draft.title: The periodic table begins
card: In 1869, the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements known at the time into a table. He ordered them by mass and grouped those with similar properties.
Mendeleev left gaps in his table for elements that had not been found yet. He used the pattern of properties to predict what the missing elements would be like.
Later, elements were discovered that matched his predictions. This gave scientists good reason to trust the table.
In the modern periodic table, metals sit on the left and non-metals sit on the right.
draft.remember: The table grouped elements by pattern, and its gaps predicted new ones.

a.q: Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in his periodic table?
opts: He expected elements not yet found to fit those spaces
He had run out of room for the elements he knew about
He wanted to separate the metals from the non-metals
He could not work out the masses of some known elements
a.why: The pattern of properties suggested that some elements were still missing, so he left spaces for them. The gaps were not about room or about sorting metals from non-metals, because the card says he ordered elements by mass and properties.
a.clue: Think about what the gaps let him predict.

b.q: Ayesha looks at a modern periodic table. Sulfur is a non-metal. Where is it most likely to be found?
opts: On the right side of the table
On the left side of the table
In a gap Mendeleev left empty
In a separate table of mixtures
b.why: Non-metals sit on the right of the modern periodic table, so sulfur is on the right. The left side is where metals sit, which is the tempting wrong answer.
b.clue: Metals are on one side, non-metals on the other.

a.best: He expected elements not yet found to fit those spaces

b.best: On the right side of the table
